CHAPTER 02 / WEBFRONT

Opening a window

Registering a C++ function and loading the development environment.

Notation conventions

Function names, types, commands, options and filenames appear in monospace, for example describe, wf test or main.cpp. Italics introduce a term at its definition. Code blocks give the fragments to enter; the preceding text states their location and prerequisites.

Registering a C++ function ↓Choosing the display frontend ↓Loading the tools ↓

Registering a C++ function

The following programme uses Life.hpp and LifeFrontend.hpp from the example. Build it within that project, where the supporting headers are available.

cppFunction registers the calculation under the name life.step. bootstrap loads the development environment and show opens the window. The path life-project identifies the directory that will hold the interface sources.

C++23
#include "Life.hpp"
#include "LifeFrontend.hpp"
#include <webfront/WebFront.hpp>

int main() {
    webfront::demo::LifeApp app{"life-project"};
    app.cppFunction("life.step", &webfront::demo::nextLife);
    app.bootstrap("developer");
    app.show();
}

Choosing the display frontend

Run examples/WebFrontLifeDeveloper from the build directory. With Visual Studio, use examples\Debug\WebFrontLifeDeveloper.exe.

The examples look for WebView2 on Windows, WKWebView on macOS 13.3 or later, and WebKitGTK 6.0 on Linux. If no native engine is available, they open the system browser.

The application type determines this choice: webfront::WebFront always uses the system browser; NativeApp selects a native window. Create and display native windows on the main thread.

Loading the tools

On its first run, the bootstrap downloads a pinned environment version and checks its SHA-512 integrity. Later runs use the local cache.

The terminal requires neither a separate Node.js installation nor a package manager on the host. It does, however, have access to the project and can execute its code. Use it with a trusted project.
